newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: Mauritania opposition wins first assembly seat.
newsitem.headline: Mauritania opposition wins first assembly seat.

text.p: A new party championing the rights of Mauritania's blacks and ex-slaves or their descendants won the opposition's first seat in the national assembly after an election run-off.

One week after the ruling Democratic and Social Republican Party won a crushing majority amid cries of fraud, results from the Interior Ministry gave Action for Change one seat in the capital Nouakchott's Sebha district in Friday's second round.
But the ruling party defeated Action for Change in the race for two seats in the Moslem West African nation's second city of Nouadibou. Results from a further two seats had yet to be announced.
The reruns followed a first round in which the ruling party won 61 of the 79 seats in the new national assembly, the second since Mauritania's 1991 democratic transition.
The first round was the first truly multi-party legislative election in the former French colony straddling Arab and black Africa.

The opposition boycotted an election in 1992, alleging widespread fraud after President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya, who seized power in a bloodless 1984 coup, won a six-year term. The ruling party won 67 of the 79 seats then.

Veteran opposition stalwart Ahmed Ould Daddah's Union of Democratic Forces-New Era party, which alleged massive fraud in last week's first round, passed up the chance of winning two seats in Nouakchott by boycotting the second round. The ruling party took both.

Action for Change, formed just over a year ago and led by former slave Messoud Ould Boulkheir, had the backing of Ould Daddah's party and the moderate Union for Democracy and Progress. Witnesses described turnout in the capital as low.
Mauritania, a nation of 2.2 million people, stands at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara Desert.
Light-skinned Moors of Arab stock and blacks each make up a third of the population, Arabic-speaking ex-slaves or Harratin the remainder. Mauritania formally banned slavery in 1980.
International observers spoke of "imperfections" in the first round, in which the opposition had been hoping to make its mark ahead of a presidential election due by January 1998.

Independents, many of them ruling party supporters denied the party ticket, contested nine seats on Friday and won at least one. An independent won one first round seat and a small party backing Taya took another.

Rivalry between Moors and black Mauritanians spilled over into tension with neighbouring Senegal and bloodshed in 1989. Migrant Moors and Harratins were killed in race riots in Senegal and there were reprisal killings in Mauritania.
The rise of Action for Change has put the racial divide, which has plagued Mauritania since independence in 1960, firmly back on the agenda.
Politicians say that for the first time the Harratin, who historically consider themselves part of the Arab community with the Moors, have made common cause with blacks from the south.
